client: I've been having a really hard time since my younger sister passed away six months ago in a car accident. It's like everything that used to make me happy just feels hollow now, and I can't seem to find any real joy in anything. And honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I had to try something.
therapist: I'm so glad you reached out, and I want you to know that what you're carrying — the loss of your sister, the emptiness that's followed — is one of the most painful things a person can go through. It makes complete sense that the things that once brought you joy feel distant right now, and your skepticism about whether talking will help is completely valid and worth honoring. Can you tell me a little about what a typical day looks like for you these days — what you find yourself doing, thinking, or feeling as you move through it?

client: Honestly, most days I just kind of go through the motions. I wake up, make coffee, sit there for way too long staring at nothing, and then feel guilty that I'm not doing more with my time. It's like there's this fog that won't lift, and by the end of the day I realize I barely spoke to anyone or did anything that felt meaningful.
therapist: What you're describing — the fog, the stillness, the guilt about the stillness — sounds really heavy and draining, like you're expending a lot of energy just to get through each day while also judging yourself for how you're getting through it. That guilt you feel about "not doing more" is something I'd gently like to explore, because grief often looks exactly like what you're describing, and yet your mind seems to be treating it as a personal failing. What do you think you *should* be doing differently, and where do you think that expectation is coming from?

client: I guess I feel like I should be... functioning more. Like, going to work without it feeling like climbing a mountain, calling my mom back, maybe even just cooking a real meal instead of eating crackers over the sink at midnight. The expectation, I think, comes from watching everyone else just keep going after loss — my coworkers, my friends — and I'm the only one still stuck in this fog weeks later, so it must mean something is wrong with me specifically.
therapist: That comparison — measuring your grief against how others appear on the outside — is such a painful and unfair standard to hold yourself to, because grief is deeply personal and rarely follows the timeline we see (or think we see) in others. I want to gently challenge that thought that something is "wrong with you specifically," because what you're describing — the fog, the difficulty functioning, the isolation — are actually very normal responses to a sudden, traumatic loss like losing your sister in an accident. What do you think you might say to a close friend who came to you six months after losing their sibling and described feeling exactly the way you do right now?

client: I know what I'd probably say to a friend — I'd tell them to be gentle with themselves, that there's no right way to grieve. But it feels completely different when it's me, like the rules don't apply the same way. I can say those words to someone else and mean them, but when I try to turn them toward myself it just feels hollow, like I'm reciting something I don't actually believe.
therapist: What you've just noticed is really important — there's a gap between what you *know* and what you can actually *feel* as true for yourself, and that gap is one of the most common and frustrating parts of grief and self-compassion work. The words feel hollow not because they're wrong, but because your mind has built up a stronger, more practiced belief that *you* are somehow the exception — and beliefs that deep don't shift just by saying the right words. I'm curious, when you try to be gentle with yourself and it feels hollow, what is the louder voice underneath that's pushing back and saying you don't deserve that gentleness?

client: I think the louder voice is saying something like... "you should have known better" or "you had every chance to fix things and you didn't." It's this constant replay of all the moments where I could have called more, visited more, just been more present with my dad before he died, and I didn't. And underneath that is this feeling that grief is something I've earned the hard way, like I don't get to feel comforted because I'm the one who caused the pain in the first place.
therapist: There's something really significant that just emerged — you mentioned your dad, and it sounds like there may be a layer of loss and guilt here that goes even deeper than your sister's passing, like you've been carrying a belief that you are somehow responsible for the pain you're in. That voice telling you that you "caused" this and therefore don't deserve comfort is one of the cruelest things grief can do — it turns your love for the people you lost into evidence against yourself, when really those regrets exist *because* you cared so deeply. I want to sit with this gently — can you tell me more about what happened with your dad, and how that loss connects to what you're feeling now?

client: I don't know if I'm ready to go into all of that right now, honestly. My dad passed about three years before my sister, and I just... I never really dealt with it properly, I think I just pushed it down and told myself I'd grieve later, and then later never came before everything fell apart again. What you said about turning love into evidence against myself, that actually kind of hit me, because I do that, I know I do that, but knowing it doesn't make it stop.
therapist: It's completely okay to leave your dad's story for when you feel ready — what you've just shared is already really meaningful, and I want to honor that boundary. You've named something profound: that knowing a pattern exists and being able to stop it are two very different things, and that gap isn't a sign of weakness — it's actually why this kind of work takes time and gentleness rather than just insight alone. What do you think it would feel like, even just a little bit, to let yourself be someone who is allowed to grieve — not because you did everything perfectly, but simply because you loved them?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. Like, I want to say "yes, of course I'm allowed to grieve," but there's this immediate voice in my head that says I don't deserve to feel sad when I'm the one who pulled away, who didn't call enough, who made it about my own discomfort. It's hard to separate "I loved them" from "but I also failed them" — they feel all tangled up together in a way that makes grief feel like something I haven't earned.
therapist: The way you've just described that — love and failure all tangled together, impossible to separate — tells me something really important: you're not grieving *less* because of those regrets, you're actually grieving *more*, carrying both the loss and a verdict against yourself at the same time. But I want to gently offer this: pulling away, not calling enough, making things hard sometimes — those are things humans do with the people they love most, often *because* the closeness feels so high-stakes, and they don't cancel out the love. What would it mean for you if it turned out that the regrets and the love could both be true at the same time — that you could have fallen short in moments *and* still deserve to grieve them fully?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it feels almost too convenient, like a way of letting myself off the hook. Because if I just accept that "humans make mistakes" and move on, what does that say about how much I actually valued him? The guilt feels like the only honest thing I have left, like giving it up would mean pretending everything was fine when it wasn't.
therapist: What you just said is so honest and so worth sitting with — the idea that guilt feels like the last truthful tribute to him, like releasing it would somehow erase the realness of what wasn't said or done. But I want to offer a gentle reframe: guilt isn't the only way to honor that something mattered — in fact, grief itself, the fog, the hollow days, the fact that you're here trying to work through this, is already profound evidence of how much you valued him. What if holding onto the guilt isn't actually keeping you close to him, but instead keeping you close to the worst version of yourself in relation to him, rather than the fuller, more complicated person who genuinely loved him?

client: That's... a lot to take in, and part of me wants to push back on it, honestly. Because if I let go of the guilt, what's left — just the grief, just the emptiness? I'm not sure that feels any better, and I guess I'm scared that without the guilt to focus on, I'll just feel completely lost and alone with it all.
therapist: What you're describing is really courageous to admit — that the guilt, as painful as it is, has actually been serving a purpose, giving you something to hold onto, a way of staying oriented when everything else feels like open, empty water. That fear of what's underneath the guilt is real and valid, and I don't want to rush you past it, because grief without a focus can feel terrifyingly formless. But I'm curious — when you imagine just the grief, without the self-blame layered on top, what do you picture that feeling actually looking like, and does any part of you sense that it might be something you could eventually bear?

client: I sit with that question for a moment, because honestly it's not one I've let myself ask before. When I try to imagine the grief without the guilt attached, it feels like... standing in a huge empty room with no walls, like there's nothing to push against, nothing to define where I end and the sadness begins. And I don't know if I could bear that, because at least the guilt feels like something solid, even if it's crushing me.
therapist: That image you just gave me — the huge empty room with no walls — is one of the most honest and vivid descriptions of grief I've heard, and I want you to know that what you're sensing isn't weakness, it's actually the real shape of the loss you've been protecting yourself from feeling. The guilt has been functioning like walls in that room, something solid to orient yourself against, and it makes complete sense that you'd be reluctant to let go of the only structure you have. I wonder, though — what if learning to bear that open, boundless feeling isn't something you'd have to do all at once, or alone, but something that could be approached slowly, with support, a little at a time?
